entries.fadad6a916c7381937f576627b7a7ca7c943ea4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12130"/><div sID="gen21967" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12130"/><hi type="bold">21. the first king--</hi>Philip was king of Macedon before Alexander, but the latter was the first who, as a generalissimo of Greece, subdued the Persian empire. <div eID="gen21967" type="x-p"/>
entries.875813b222713b0c7fa75b40a015abb4c5f6c968: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12131"/><div sID="gen21968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12131"/><hi type="bold">22. not in his power--</hi>not with the power which Alexander possessed [Maurer]. An empire united, as under Alexander, is more powerful than one divided, as under the four Diadochi. <div eID="gen21968" type="x-p"/>
entries.b410a16e5a4731640eea87af7b947c40aed4b9ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12132"/><div sID="gen21969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12132"/><hi type="bold">23. transgressors are come to the full--</hi>This does not hold good of the times of Antiochus, but of the closing times of the Christian era. Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.18.8">Lu 18:8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1-2Tim.3.9">2Ti 3:1-9</reference>, as to the wickedness of the world in general just before Christ's second coming. Israel's guilt, too, shall then be at the full, when they who rejected Christ shall receive Antichrist; fulfilling Jesus words, "I am come in My Father's name, and ye receive Me not; if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive" (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Ge 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.32">Mt 23:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1Th 2:16</reference>).<div eID="gen21969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of fierce countenance--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.28.50">De 28:50</reference>); one who will spare neither old nor young.<div eID="gen21970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understanding dark sentences--</hi>rather, "artifices" [Gesenius]. Antiochus made himself master of Egypt and Jerusalem successively by craft (1 Maccabees 1:30, &c.; 2 Maccabees 5:24, &c.). <div eID="gen21971" type="x-p"/>
entries.4718d6116cceb32cd778dc86b6efc75df43106a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12133"/><div sID="gen21972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12133"/><hi type="bold">24. not by his own power--</hi>which in the beginning was "little" (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">7:8</reference>); but by gaining over others through craft, the once little horn became "mighty" (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.8.25">Da 8:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.23">11:23</reference>). To be fully realized by Antichrist. He shall act by the power of Satan, who shall then be permitted to work through him in unrestricted license, such as he has not now (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.2">Re 13:2</reference>); hence the ten kingdoms shall give the beast their power (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9-2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:9-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.13">Re 17:13</reference>).<div eID="gen21972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prosper and practise--</hi>prosper in all that he attempts (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Da 8:12</reference>).<div eID="gen21973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy people--</hi>His persecutions are especially directed against the Jews. <div eID="gen21974" type="x-p"/>
entries.8be3f71e4ddd1f5ca8ee08735ea22c23175bf398: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12134"/><div sID="gen21975" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12134"/><hi type="bold">25. by peace--</hi>by pretending "peace" and friendship; in the midst of security [Gesenius], suddenly striking his blow (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">Jr 15:8</reference>). "A spoiler at noon-day."<div eID="gen21975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also ... against the Prince of princes--</hi>not merely against the Jews (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.11">Da 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">11:36</reference>).<div eID="gen21976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">broken without hand--</hi>by God's special visitation. The stone "cut out of the mountain without hands," that is, Christ is to smite the world power image on his feet (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>), that is, in its last development (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.7.11">Da 7:11</reference>). Antiochus' horrible death by worms and ulcers, when on his way to Judea, intending to take vengeance for the defeat of his armies by the Maccabees, was a primary fulfilment, foreshadowing God's judgment on the last enemy of the Jewish Church. <div eID="gen21977" type="x-p"/>
entries.898aa22311ddacf31c672b9a4b6d4db11068e37b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12135"/><div sID="gen21978" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12135"/><hi type="bold">26. shut ... up ... vision--</hi>implying the vision was not to be understood for the present. In <reference osisRef="Rev.22.10">Re 22:10</reference> it is said, "Seal not the vision, for the time is at hand." What in Daniel's time was hidden was more fully explained in Revelation, and as the time draws nearer, it will be clearer still.<div eID="gen21978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall be for many days--</hi>It refers to remote times (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.27">Eze 12:27</reference>). <div eID="gen21979" type="x-p"/>
entries.69ebd333c4f1daf3a0b9bf99f76c50718de933cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12136"/><div sID="gen21980" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12136"/><hi type="bold">27. I ... was sick--</hi>through grief at the calamities coming on my people and the Church of God (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.102.14">Psa 102:14</reference>).<div eID="gen21980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">afterward I ... did the king's business--</hi>He who holds nearest communion with heaven can best discharge the duties of common life.<div eID="gen21981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none understood it--</hi>He had heard of kings, but knew not their names; He foresaw the events, but not the time when they were to take place; thereupon he could only feel "astonished," and leave all with the omniscient God [Jerome]. <chapter eID="Dan.8"/>

entries.1b28c5d4582043b0fb6849ef2cc91757793997f2: <div eID="gen33164" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33165" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33166" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33166" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33165" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33167" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains Daniel's vision of the ram and he-goat, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.1-Dan.8.14">Dan 8:1-14</reference>; referring, as explained by the angel, to the Persian and Grecian monarchies, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.15-Dan.8.26">Dan 8:15-26</reference>. The little horn mentioned in the ninth verse, (or fierce king, as interpreted in the twenty-third), is supposed by some to denote Antiochus Epiphanes; but seems more properly to apply to the Roman power in general, by which the polity and temple of the Jews were destroyed, on account of the great transgressions of these ancient people of God; and particularly because of their very obstinate and unaccountable rejection of the glorious doctrines of Christianity, which had been preached among them by Jesus Christ and his apostles, and the truth of which God had attested "by signs and wonders, and by divers miracles and gifts of the Holy Ghost." Daniel is then informed of the two thousand and three hundred prophetic days (that is, years) which must elapse before the sanctuary be cleansed; or, in other words, before righteousness shall prevail over the whole earth. This period is supposed, with considerable probability to have had its commencement when Alexander the Great invaded Asia, in the year before Christ 334. This will bring the close of it to about the end of the Sixth chiliad of the world; when, as already observed, some astonishing changes are expected to take place in the moral condition of the human race; when the power of Antichrist, both Papal and Mohammedan, shall be totally annihilated, and universal dominion given to the saints of the Most High. The chapter concludes with the distress of Daniel on account of the fearful judgments with which his country should be visited in after ages, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.27">Dan 8:27</reference>. <div eID="gen33167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33168" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33169" type="x-p"/> In the third year of the reign of - Belshazzar - We now come once more to the Hebrew, the Chaldee part of the book being finished. As the Chaldeans had a particular interest both in the history and prophecies from <reference osisRef="Dan.2.4">Dan 2:4</reference> to the end of chap. 7, the whole is written in Chaldee, but as the prophecies which remain concern times posterior to the Chaldean monarchy, and principally relate to the Church and people of God generally, they are written in the Hebrew language, this being the tongue in which God chose to reveal all his counsels given under the Old Testament relative to the New.
entries.af337365fcd6b9f549225f51337d558236c95a5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33170" type="x-p"/> I saw in a vision - Daniel was at this time in Shushan, which appears to have been a strong place, where the kings of Persia had their summer residence. It was the capital of the province of Elam or the Elymais; which province was most probably added to the Chaldean territories by Nebuchadnezzar; see <reference osisRef="Jer.49.34">Jer 49:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.35">Jer 49:35</reference>. Here was Daniel's ordinary residence; and though here at this time, he, in vision, saw himself on the banks of the river Ulai. This is the same as the river Euleus, which divided Shushan or Susiana from Elymais.
entries.ca52f9660618903980ad5c7bafbb37a4f48327a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33171" type="x-p"/> A ram which had two horns - In the former vision there were four beasts, pointing out four empires; in this we have but two, as only two empires are concerned here, viz., the Grecian and the Persian. The Babylonish empire is not mentioned; its fate was before decided, and it was now at its close. <div eID="gen33171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33172" type="x-p"/> By the ram, the empire of the Medes and Persians was pointed out, as explained by the angel Gabriel, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.20">Dan 8:20</reference>; and particularly Cyrus, who was the founder of that empire. Cyrus was the son of Cambyses, king of Persia; and grandson of Astyages, king of Media, by his daughter Mandane, who had been given in marriage to Cambyses. Cyrus marrying Roxana, the daughter and only child of his uncle Cyaxares, called in Scripture Ahasuerus, succeeded to both crowns, and thus united Media and Persia. A ram was the symbol of the Persians; and a ram's head with two horns, one higher than the other, appears as such in different parts of the ruins of Persepolis. See the plates of these ruins in the supplement to the seventh volume of the ancient part of the Universal History. <div eID="gen33172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33173" type="x-p"/> This ram had two horns; that is, two kingdoms, viz., Media and Persia; but one was higher than the other; and the higher came up last. Media, signified by the shorter horn, was the more ancient of the two kingdoms. Persia, the higher horn, had come up but lately, and was of little historic or political consequence till the time of Cyrus; but in the reigns of this prince and his immediate successors, Persia attained a political consequence greatly superior to that possessed at any time by the kingdom of Media; therefore, it is said to have been the higher, and to have come up last.
entries.952e1d0299861e09f328448c9215ca6443ea85a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33174" type="x-p"/> I saw the ram pushing westward - The Persians, who are signified by the ram, as well as their founder Cyrus, pushed their conquests west, north and south. The principal theater of their wars, says Calmet, was against the Scythians, northward; against the Greeks, westward; and against the Egyptians, southward. <div eID="gen33174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33175" type="x-p"/> He did according to his will - There was no other nation at that time that could stay the progress of the Persian arms.
entries.95886fb5ee09d3d7cbfe94d9433a1c1d81830580: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33176" type="x-p"/> Behold, a he-goat - This was Alexander the Great; and a goat was a very proper symbol of the Grecian or Macedonian people. Bp. Newton very properly observes that, two hundred years before the time of Daniel, they were called Aegeadae, the goats' people; the origin of which name is said to be as follows: Caranus, their first king, going with a multitude of Greeks to seek a new habitation in Macedonia, was advised by an oracle to take the goats for his guides; and afterwards, seeing a herd of goats flying from a violent storm, he followed them to Edessa, and there fixed the seat of his empire, and made the goats his ensigns or standards; and called the place Aege or Aegea, the goats' town; and the people Aegeadae, the goats' people; names which are derived from αιξ, αιγος, a goat. The city Aege or Aegea, was the usual burying-place of the Macedonian kings; and, in reference to this origin, Alexander called his son by Roxana, Alexander Aegus, Alexander the goat. All this shows the very great propriety of the symbol here used. <div eID="gen33176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33177" type="x-p"/> Came from the west - Europe lies westward of Asia. <div eID="gen33177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33178" type="x-p"/> On the face of the whole earth - Carrying every thing before him. <div eID="gen33178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33179" type="x-p"/> Touched not the ground - Seemed to fly from conquest to conquest. By the time Alexander was thirty years of age he had conquered all Asia: and, because of the rapidity of his conquests, he is represented as a leopard with four wings, in the preceding vision. <div eID="gen33179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33180" type="x-p"/> A notable horn between his eyes - This, says the angel, is the first king, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.21">Dan 8:21</reference>, that is, the first kingdom of the Greeks in Asia, which was erected by Alexander; and continued some years in his brother Philip Aridaeus, and in his two young sons, Alexander Aegus and Hercules. See Newton.
entries.f2a828464df3bf0c533d4cb5b50a829478199115: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33181" type="x-p"/> And he came to the ram - This and the following verse give an account of the overthrow of the Persian empire by Alexander. <div eID="gen33181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33182" type="x-p"/> And ran unto him in the fury of his power - The conflicts between the Greeks and the Persians were excessively severe. Alexander first vanquished the generals of Darius, at the river Granicus, in Phrygia; he next attacked and totally routed Darius, at the straits of Issus, in Cilicia; and afterwards at the plains of Arbela, in Assyria. One can hardly read these words, says Bp. Newton, "the ram - which I had seen standing by the river, ran unto him in the fury of his power," without having the image of Darius' army standing and guarding the river Granicus and of Alexander on the other side, with his forces plunging in swimming across the stream, and rushing on the enemy, with all the fire and fury that can be conceived.
entries.0e5762f848ca45fd8baed81a2e76d1c5748b635e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33183" type="x-p"/> And brake his two horns - Subdued Persia and Media; sacked and burnt the royal city of Persepolis, the capital of the Persian empire, and, even in its ruins, one of the wonders of the world to the present day. This he did because "he was moved with choler" against Darius, who had endeavored to draw off his captains with bribes, and had labored to induce some of his friends to assassinate him. Alexander, finding this, would listen to no proposals of peace; and was determined never to rest till he had destroyed Darius and his whole empire. In Media, Darius was seized and made prisoner by some of his own treacherous subjects, and afterwards basely murdered. <div eID="gen33183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33184" type="x-p"/> There was no power in the ram to stand before him - Alexander's victories over the Persians were as easy as they were rapid and decisive. <div eID="gen33184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33185" type="x-p"/> He cast him down to the ground, and stamped upon him - Totally destroyed the family, and overturned the whole monarchy.
entries.eeb0a37f68a8f6ff2db6a3f3a371fe0a487d651e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33186" type="x-p"/> The he-goat waxed very strong - He had subdued nearly the whole of the then known world. <div eID="gen33186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33187" type="x-p"/> The great horn was broken - Alexander died in the height of his conquests, when he was but about thirty-three years of age. His natural brother, Philip Aridaeus, and his two sons, Alexander Aegus and Hercules, kept up the show and name of the Macedonian kingdom for a time; but they were all murdered within fifteen years; and thus the great horn, the Macedonian kingdom, was broken, Alexander's family being now cut off. <div eID="gen33187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33188" type="x-p"/> And for it came up four notable ones - The regal family being all dead, the governors of provinces usurped the title of kings; and Antigonus, one of them, being slain at the battle of Ipsus, they were reduced to four, as we have already seen. <div eID="gen33188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33189" type="x-p"/> 1. Seleucus, who had Syria and Babylon, from whom came the Seleucidae, famous in history. <div eID="gen33189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33190" type="x-p"/> 2. Lysimachus, who had Asia Minor. <div eID="gen33190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33191" type="x-p"/> 3. Ptolemy, son of Lagus, who had Egypt, from whom sprang the Lagidae. And, <div eID="gen33191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33192" type="x-p"/> 4. Cassander, who had Greece and the neighboring countries. These held dominion towards the four winds of heaven. <div eID="gen33192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33193" type="x-p"/> Cassander had the western parts, Lysimachus had the northern regions, Ptolemy possessed the southern countries, and Seleucus had the eastern provinces.
entries.d5ae1a003dc7c6be78f6db019e8aac9ca95bb543: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33194" type="x-p"/> Out of one of them came forth a little horn - Some think that Antiochus Epiphanes is meant; but Bp. Newton contends that it is the Roman government that is intended; and although very great at its zenith, yet very little in its rising. <div eID="gen33194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33195" type="x-p"/> Waxed - great toward the south - The Romans made Egypt a province of their empire, and it continued such for some centuries. <div eID="gen33195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33196" type="x-p"/> Toward the east - They conquered Syria, and made it a province. <div eID="gen33196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33197" type="x-p"/> Toward the pleasant land - Judea, so called <reference osisRef="Psa.106.24">Psa 106:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jer 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">Dan 11:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.41">Dan 11:41</reference>. It is well known that they took Judea, and made it a province; and afterwards burnt the city and the temple, and scattered the Jews over the face of the earth.
entries.56389245999c0b6c94958ec584cf67678f0c5008: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33198" type="x-p"/> The host of heaven - The Jewish hierarchy. The stars, the priests and Levites. The powers or host of heaven are probably intended by our Lord, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.29">Mat 24:29</reference>, to signify the whole Jewish hierarchy.
entries.de9ffd76aa7b2f5b027a9e1a57f3a4cc1be8bd24: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33199" type="x-p"/> Even to the prince of the host - They seemed, in this case, to fight against God himself. <div eID="gen33199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33200" type="x-p"/> The daily sacrifice was taken away - By the destruction of the city and temple; and has never been restored from that day until now.
entries.391984594f56a5f0881deea7bb3093f138f7ded7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33201" type="x-p"/> And a host was given him - That is, power; or perhaps the host of heaven - the priesthood - the whole sacrificial system, by reason of transgression. They had filled up the measure of their iniquities, in rejecting the Lord that bought them; and the daily sacrifice, being no longer of use, was given up with the rest to destruction. <div eID="gen33201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33202" type="x-p"/> Cast down the truth - Probably the whole Jewish ritual and religion. <div eID="gen33202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33203" type="x-p"/> Practiced, and prospered - Prosperity or success followed all their acts.
entries.ba15d23cc1d7e29f667f58264be6e1c813fdf3dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33204" type="x-p"/> One saint speaking, and another saint said - One angel asked another how long the sanctuary was to be trodden down?
entries.83b75517ff9723fd6af67ac0696c67952741b45d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33205" type="x-p"/> Unto two thousand and three hundred days - Though literally it be two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings. Yet I think the prophetic day should be understood here, as in other parts of this prophet, and must signify so many years. If we date these years from the vision of the he-goat, (Alexander's invading Asia), this was A.M. 3670, b.c. 334; and two thousand three hundred years from that time will reach to a.d. 1966, or one hundred and forty-one years from the present a.d. 1825. This will bring it near to the time mentioned <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Dan 7:25</reference> (note), where see the note.
entries.b0c5a93b46a80146c7671b1455cb011f303c1ea8: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen33205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33206" type="x-p"/> As the appearance of a man - Supposed to be the Messiah.
entries.dcba5c1c565d4627e5bf9cf6f3c1702fd1cb98b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen33206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33207" type="x-p"/> At the time of the end shall be the vision - Or, as Houbigant, "The vision shall have an end at the proper time."
entries.db19420a755403c420b730091656f406b5e1b05e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen33207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33208" type="x-p"/> The ram which thou sagest - See this explained under the vision itself, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.3">Dan 8:3</reference> (note), etc.
entries.6af3464eeb985f73b69e4e031140e5878134bd64: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen33208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33209" type="x-p"/> But not in his power - The four kingdoms which shall arise out of the Macedonian empire shall not be of Alexander's power or family, nor have his strength and dignity.
entries.869c246f260d5d860b7f6f552ddf89c3251878e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen33209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33210" type="x-p"/> When the transgressors are come to the full - When the utmost degradation has taken place, by the buying and selling of the high priesthood; for Onias was ejected for a sum of money, to make room for wicked Jason; and Jason again was supplanted for a greater sum by a worse man, if possible, than himself, Menelaus; and the golden vessels of the temple were sold to pay for this sacrilegious purchase. Thus transgressions were come to the full, before the Romans had commission to destroy Jerusalem and its temple, etc. <div eID="gen33210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33211" type="x-p"/> A king of fierce countenance - The Roman government, as before; for king is often taken for kingdom or empire. <div eID="gen33211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33212" type="x-p"/> Understanding dark sentences - Very learned and skillful in all things relating to government and its intrigues. The learning of Rome is proverbial to the present time.
entries.24efdedd6e1582f8510957da3b4194fe90427cd2: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen33212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33213" type="x-p"/> But not by his own power - The strength of the other kingdoms consisted in themselves; but the Roman empire, as a horn or kingdom of the goat, was not mighty by its own power - was not strong by virtue of the goat, but drew its nourishment and strength from Rome and Italy. There grew the trunk and body of the tree; though the branches extended over Greece, Asia, Syria, and Egypt. - Bp. Newton. <div eID="gen33213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33214" type="x-p"/> Shall destroy wonderfully - In the taking of Jerusalem by the Romans ninety-seven thousand Jews were made captives, and eleven hundred thousand were slain. So they destroyed this once mighty and holy people!
entries.1ab0bd7efee76e2881d92eb0cfc2726e264c0442: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen33214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33215" type="x-p"/> He shall cause craft to prosper - They subdued as many by their diplomatic skill and political intrigues as they did by the sword. <div eID="gen33215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33216" type="x-p"/> He shall also stand up against the Prince of princes - Against Christ, for it was by the Roman authority that he was condemned to death and crucified; and their persecutions had nearly destroyed the Christian religion; but the house was founded on a rock. <div eID="gen33216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33217" type="x-p"/> But he shall be broken without hand - The tide was turned by the invisible hand of God; and thus heathen Rome was overcome, and converted to Christianity. <div eID="gen33217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33218" type="x-p"/> The vision of the evening and the morning which was told is true - That mentioned in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.14">Dan 8:14</reference>. <div eID="gen33218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33219" type="x-p"/> For it shall be for many days - Not less than two thousand three hundred years!

entries.5de04849781c5003b228b5e50c3a3b489f4523eb: <div eID="gen15806" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Part Second - The Development of the Kingdom of God - <reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Daniel 8-12</reference></title> <div sID="gen15807" type="x-p"/> This Part contains three revelations which Daniel received during the reigns of Belshazzar, Darius the Mede, and Cyrus the Persian, regarding the development of the kingdom of God. After describing in the First Part the development of the world-power and its relation to the people and kingdom of God from the days of Nebuchadnezzar, its founder, down to the time of its final destruction by the perfected kingdom of God, in this Second Part it is revealed to the prophet how the kingdom of God, in war against the power and enmity of the rulers of the world, and amid severe oppressions, is carried forward to final victory and is perfected. <div eID="gen15807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15808" type="x-p"/> The first vision, Daniel 8, represents what will happen to the people of God during the developments of the second and third world-kingdoms. The second revelation, Daniel 9, gives to the prophet, in answer to his penitential prayer for the restoration of the ruined holy city and the desolated sanctuary, disclosures regarding the whole development of the kingdom of God, from the close of the Babylonish exile to the final accomplishment of God’s plan of salvation. In the last vision, in the third year of Cyrus, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.12">Daniel 10-12</reference>, he received yet further and more special revelations regarding the severe persecutions which await the people of God for their purification, in the nearer future under Antiochus Epiphanes, and in the time of the end under the last foe, the Antichrist. <div eID="gen15808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15809" type="x-p"/> At Susa, in the province of Elam, Daniel saw in vision (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.1">Dan 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.2">Dan 8:2</reference>) a ram with two horns, which a he-goat coming from the west, running over the earth, having a great horn on his brow, smote and destroyed (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.3-Dan.8.7">Dan 8:3-7</reference>). After that the goat waxed very mighty, till his great horn was broken; and in its place four notable horns grew up toward the four winds of heaven, and out of one of them there came forth a little horn, which directed its might toward the south and the east and toward the holy land, contended against the host of heaven, and magnified itself to the Prince of the heavenly host, took away the daily sacrifice, and desolated the place of the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.8-Dan.8.12">Dan 8:8-12</reference>). He then hears from an angel how long this sacrilege shall continue (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.14">Dan 8:14</reference>). Another angel thereafter gives him an explanation (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.15-Dan.8.26">Dan 8:15-26</reference>) of the vision; and with a remark (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.27">Dan 8:27</reference>) regarding the effect of this revelation on the mind of Daniel, the chapter closes. <div eID="gen15809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15810" type="x-p"/> This vision, it is manifest from the definition of the time in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.1">Dan 8:1</reference>, stands in relation to the vision of the foregoing chapter, and in its contents is united to it also in so far as it gives more particular revelations regarding the relations of the second and third world-kingdoms, which are only briefly set forth in Daniel 7. But notwithstanding this point of union, this chapter does not form a mere appendix to the foregoing, but gives a new revelation regarding a phase in the development of the world-power and its enmity against the people of God of which nothing is prophesied in Daniel 7. The opinion that this chapter forms only an appendix to Daniel 7 is based on the erroneous idea that the fourth world-kingdom, the Macedonian, and the little horn in Daniel 7 are identical with that prophesied of in this chapter.<note placement="foot">According to the modern critics (Berth., v. Leng., Hitz., Bleek), this chapter must have been written shortly before the re-consecration of the temple, or immediately thereafter, before or immediately after the death of Antiochus Epiphanes. This supposition is drawn from <reference osisRef="Dan.8.14">Dan 8:14</reference>, according to which the period of oppression shall continue 2300 evening-mornings. But, overlooking the circumstance that these critics cannot agree as to the reckoning of this period of time, and thus announce the uncertainty of their hypothesis, the whole of the other contents of the chapter stand in contradiction to this supposition. It contains no hint whatever of the great victories of the Maccabees which preceded the consecration of the temple, and first made it possible, but, on the contrary, speaks of the oppression as continuing unchanged till the oppressor is himself destroyed (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.25">Dan 8:25</reference>), and then it breaks off without any Messianic view, as one should expect from a parenetic poem of a Maccabean Jews; so that Bleek finds himself compelled from his own resources to add “the intimation, that the beginning of the deliverance destined by God for His people is closely and immediately joined to the discontinuance of the worship of Jehovah by Antioch. Epiph., and to the destruction of this prince,” in order to give to the vision “a Messianic character.”</note> <div eID="gen15810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15811" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Dan.8.1-Dan.8.7">Dan 8:1-7</reference> <div eID="gen15811" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Vision</title> <div sID="gen15812" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Dan.8.1">Dan 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.2">Dan 8:2</reference> contain the historical introduction to this new revelation. This was given to Daniel in the third year of the reign of Belshazzar, and thus two years after the vision of the four world-kingdoms (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.1">Dan 7:1</reference>), but not in a dream as that was, but while he was awake. The words, <hi type="italic">I, Daniel</hi>, are neither a pleonasm (Häv.) nor a sign that the writer wished specially to give himself out for Daniel (Ewald), but expressly denote that Daniel continues to speak of himself in the first person (Kliefoth). The article in הנראה (<hi type="italic">that which appeared</hi>) takes place of the relative אשׁר, and the expression is concise for נראה אשׁר החזון (<hi type="italic">the vision which appeared</hi>); cf. Ewald’s <hi type="italic">Lehr</hi>. §335 <hi type="italic">a</hi>. בּתּחלּה (<hi type="italic">at the first</hi>), as in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan 9:21</reference>, in the general signification <hi type="italic">earlier</hi>, and in <reference osisRef="Gen.13.3">Gen 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.41.21">Gen 41:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.18">Gen 43:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.43.20">Gen 43:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa 1:26</reference>, synonymous with בּראשׁנה (<hi type="italic">in the beginning</hi>). Here the word points back to Daniel 7, and in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan 9:21</reference> it refers to <reference osisRef="Dan.8.16">Dan 8:16</reference> of this chapter. “In vision,” i.e., ἐν πνεύματι, not ἐν σώματι, Daniel was placed in the city of Susa, in the province of Elam (Elymaïs). By the words, “I saw in vision; and it came to pass when I saw,” which precede the specification of the scene of the vision, is indicated the fact that he was in Susa only in vision, and the misconception is sufficiently guarded against that Daniel was actually there in the body. This is acknowledge by v. Leng., Hitzig, Maurer, Häv., Hgstb., Kran., and Kliefoth, against Bertholdt and Rosenmüller, who understand this, in connection with <reference osisRef="Dan.8.27">Dan 8:27</reference>, as meaning that Daniel was personally present in Susa to execute the king’s business, from which Bertholdt frames the charge against the pseudo-Daniel, that he was not conscious that Elam under Nabonned did not belong to Babylon, and that the royal palace at Susa had as yet no existence. But this accusation has no historical foundation. We have no accurate information whether under Belshazzar Elam was added to Babylon or the Chaldean empire. It is true that not Hengstenberg (<hi type="italic">Beitr.</hi> i. p. 42f.) only has, with older theologians, concluded from the prophecies of Jer 49:34., compared with <reference osisRef="Jer.25.25">Jer 25:25</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.24">Eze 32:24</reference>, that Nebuchadnezzar subjugated Susa, but Niebuhr also (<hi type="italic">Gesch. Assurs</hi>, p. 211ff.) seeks from these and other passages of the O.T. to establish the view, that Nebuchadnezzar, after the death of Cyaxares (Uwakhshatra), to whom he owed allegiance, refused to do homage to his successor, and entered on a war against Media, which resulted in the annexation of Elam to his kingdom. But, on the contrary, Hävernick has well remarked, that the subjugation of Elam by Nebuchadnezzar can scarcely harmonize with the fact of the division of the Assyrian kingdom between the Babylonian king Nabopolassar and the Median king Cyaxares, whereby the former obtained the western and the latter the eastern half, and that from these passages of prophecy a subjugation of Elam by the Chaldeans cannot be concluded. Jeremiah announces neither in <reference osisRef="Jer.25.25">Jer 25:25</reference> nor in Jer 49:34. a conquest of Elam by Nebuchadnezzar, but rather in Jer. 49 prophesies the complete destruction of Elam, or a divine judgment, in language which is much too strong and elevated for a mere making of it tributary and annexing it to a new state. <div eID="gen15812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15813" type="x-p"/> Besides, this passage in no respect requires that Susa and Elam should be regarded as provinces of the Chaldean kingdom, since the opinion that Daniel was in Susa engaged in some public business for the Chaldean king is founded only on a false interpretation of <reference osisRef="Dan.8.2">Dan 8:2</reference>, Dan 8:27. From the prophet’s having been placed in an ecstasy in the city of Susa, there follows nothing further than that this city was already at the time of the existing Chaldean kingdom a central-point of Elamitish or Persian power. And the more definite description of the situation of this city in the words, “which was in the province of Elam,” points decidedly to the time of Daniel, in which Susa as yet belonged to the province of Elam, while this province was made a satrapy, Susis, Susiana, now Chusistan, by the kings of Persia, and Susa became the capital of this province; therefore the capital Susa is not reckoned as situated in Elam by writers, who after this time distinguish between Susis (Susiana) and Elymaïs (Elam), as Strabo, xvi. 1. 17f., Pliny, <hi type="italic">hist. nat.</hi> vi. 27: <hi type="italic">Susianen ab Elymaide disterminat amnis Eulaeus</hi>. <div eID="gen15813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15814" type="x-p"/> Still more groundless is the assertion, that the city of Susa was not in existence in the time of Daniel, or, as Duncker (<hi type="italic">Gesch. der Alterth.</hi> ii. p. 913, 3 Auf.) affirms, that Darius first removed the residence or seat of the king to Susa with the intention that it should become the permanent residence for him and his successors, the central-point of his kingdom and of his government, and that Pliny and Aelian say decidedly that Darius built Susa, the king’s city of Persia, and that the inscriptions confirm this saying. For, to begin with the latter statement, an inscription found in the ruins of a palace at Susa, according to the deciphering of Mordtmann (<hi type="italic">in der D. morgl. Ztschr</hi>. xvi. pp. 123ff.), which Duncker cites as confirming his statement, contains only these words: “Thus speaks Artaxerxes the great king, the son of Darius the son of Achämenides Vistaçpa: This building my great-great-grandfather Darius erected; afterwards it was improved by Artaxerxes my grandfather.” This inscription thus confirms only the fact of the building of a palace in Susa by Darius, but nothing further, from which it is impossible to conclude that Darius first founded the city, or built the first tower in it. Still less does such an idea lie in the words of Aelian, <hi type="italic">nat. animal</hi>. i. 59: “Darius was proud of the erection of a celebrated building which he had raised in Susa.” And Pliny also, taken strictly, speaks only of the elevation of Susa to the rank of capital of the kingdom by Darius, which does not exclude the opinion that Susa was before this already a considerable town, and had a royal castle, in which Cyrus may have resided during several months of the year (according to Xenophon, <hi type="italic">Cyrop.</hi> viii. 6. 22, <hi type="italic">Anab.</hi> iii. 5. 15; cf. Brissonius, <hi type="italic">de regio Pers. princ.</hi> p. 88f.).<note placement="foot">Pliny, <hi type="italic">hist. nat.</hi> vi. 27, says regarding <hi type="italic">Susiana</hi>, “<hi type="italic">In qua vetus regia Presarum Susa a Dario Hystaspis filio condita,</hi>” which may be understood as if he ascribed to Darius the founding of the city of Susa. But how little weight is to be given to this statement appears from the similar statement, <hi type="italic">hist. nat.</hi> vi. 14 (17): “<hi type="italic">Ecbatana caput Mediae Seleucus rex condidit,</hi>” which plainly contains an error, since Ecbatana, under the name of <hi type="italic">Achmeta</hi>, is mentioned (Ezr 6:2) in the time of Darius Hystaspes, in the tower of which the archives of the Persian kings were preserved.</note> <div eID="gen15814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15815" type="x-p"/> The founding of Susa, and of the old tower in Susa, reaches back into pre-historic times. According to Strabo, xv. 2. 3, Susa must have been built by Tithonos, the father of Memnon. With this the epithet Μεμνόνια Σοῦσα, which Herod. vii. 151, v. 54, 53, and Aelian, <hi type="italic">nat. anim</hi>. xiii. 18, gives to the town of Susa, stands in unison. For if this proves nothing more than that in Susa there was a tomb of Memnon (Häv.), yet would this sufficiently prove that the city or its citadel existed from ancient times - times so ancient that the mythic Memnon lived and was buried there. <div eID="gen15815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15816" type="x-p"/> The city had its name שׁוּשׁן, <hi type="italic">Lily</hi>, from the lilies which grew in great abundance in that region (Athen. <hi type="italic">Deipnos</hi>. xii. p. 409; Stephan. Byz., etc.), and had, according to Strabo, xv. 3. 2, a circuit of 120 (twelve English miles), and according to others, 200 stadia. Its palace was called <hi type="italic">Memnoneion</hi>, and was strongly fortified. Here was “the golden seat;” here also were “the apartments of Darius, which were adorned with gold,” as Aeschylos says (<hi type="italic">Pers</hi>. 3. 4. 159, 160), “the widely-famed palace,” - the περιβόητα βασιλεῖα, as Diod. Sic. xvii. 65, expresses himself. <div eID="gen15816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15817" type="x-p"/> The ruins of Susa are not only a wilderness, inhabited by lions and hyaenas, on the eastern banks of the Shapur, between it and the Dizful, where three great mountains of ruins, from 80 to 100 feet high, raise themselves, showing the compass of the city, while eastward smaller heaps of ruins point out the remains of the city, which to this day bear the name <hi type="italic">Schusch</hi>; cf. Herz.'s <hi type="italic">Realenc</hi>. xvi. p. 263f., and Duncker, <hi type="italic">Gesch. d. Alt</hi>. ii. p. 942ff. <div eID="gen15817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15818" type="x-p"/> The designation of Elam as מדינה, a <hi type="italic">province</hi>, does not refer to a Chaldean province. עילם, in Greek  ̓Ελυμαΐ́ς, formed the western part of the Persian satrapy of Susis or Susiana, which lay at the foot of the highlands of Iran, at the beginning of the valley of the Tigris and the Euphrates between Persia and Babylon, called by the Persians <hi type="italic">Uvaja</hi>, and by the Greeks <hi type="italic">Susis</hi> or <hi type="italic">Susiana</hi> after the capital, or <hi type="italic">Cissia</hi> after its inhabitants. It is bounded by the western border mountains of Persia and the Tigris, and on the south terminates in a arm, swampy and harbourless coast, which stretches from the mouth of the Tigris to that of the Aurvaiti (Oroatis). Strabo (xv. 732) says Susiana is inhabited by two races, the Cissaei and the Elymäi; Herodotus (iii. 91, v. 49, vii. 62), on the contrary, names only the Cissaei as the inhabitants of the country of the same name. The saying put into circulation by Josephus (<hi type="italic">Antt.</hi> i. 6. 4,  ̓́Ελαμος γὰρ  ̓Ελαμαίους Περσῶν ὄντας ἀρχηγέτας κατέλιπεν), that the Elamites are the primitive race of the Persians, has no historical foundation. The deep valley of the Tigris and the Euphrates was the country of the Semites. “The names of the towns and rivers of the country confirm the statements of Genesis, which names Elam among the sons of Shem, although the erecting of the Persian royal residence in Elam, and the long continuance of the Persian rule, could not but exercise, as it did, an influence on the manners and arts of the Semitish inhabitants” (Duncker, p. 942). <div eID="gen15818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15819" type="x-p"/> The further statement, that Daniel in vision was by the river <hi type="italic">Ulai</hi>, shows that Susa lay on the banks of the river. אוּלי is the Εὐλαῖος, <hi type="italic">Eulaeus</hi>, of the Greeks and Romans, of which Pliny says, “<hi type="italic">circuit arcem Susorum</hi>,” and which Arrian (<hi type="italic">Exped. Alex</hi>. vii. 7) also mentions as a navigable river of Susis. On the contrary, Herodotus, i. 188, v. 49, 52, and Strabo, xv. 3, 4, place Susa on the river <hi type="italic">Choaspes</hi>. These contradictory statements are reconciled in the simplest manner by the supposition that <hi type="italic">Ulai, Eulaeus</hi>, was the Semitish, <hi type="italic">Choaspes</hi> the Aryan (Persian) name of the <hi type="italic">Kuran</hi>, which received the Shapur and Dizful. In favour of this, we have not only the circumstance that the name <hi type="italic">Choaspes</hi> is undoubtedly of Persian origin, while, on the other hand, אוּלי is a word of Semitic formation; but still more, that Herodotus knows nothing whatever of the <hi type="italic">Eulaeus</hi>, while Ptolemy (vi. 3. 2) does not mention the <hi type="italic">Choaspes</hi>, but, on the contrary, two sources of the <hi type="italic">Eulaeus</hi>, the one in Media, the other in Susiana; and that what Herod. i. 188, says of the Choaspes, that the kings of Persia drink its water only, and caused it to be carried far after them, is mentioned by Pliny of the Euläus, <hi type="italic">h. n.</hi> vi. 27, and in 31:3 of the Choaspes and Euläus.<note placement="foot">There is little probability in the supposition that <hi type="italic">Choaspes</hi> is the modern <hi type="italic">Kerrah</hi> or <hi type="italic">Kerkha</hi>, the <hi type="italic">Euläus</hi> the modern <hi type="italic">Dizful</hi>, as Susa lay between these two rivers (Ker Porter, Winer, Ruetschi in Herz.'s <hi type="italic">Realen</hi>. xv. 246), and receives no sufficient support from the bas relief of Kojundshik discovered by Layard, which represents the siege of a town lying between two rivers, since the identification of this town with Susa is a mere conjecture.</note> <div eID="gen15819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15820" type="x-p"/> Daniel was in spirit conveyed to Susa, that here in the future royal citadel of the Persian kingdom he might witness the destruction of this world-power, as Ezekiel was removed to Jerusalem that he might there see the judgment of its destruction. The placing of the prophet also on the river of Ulai is significant, yet it is not to be explained, with Kranichfeld, from <reference osisRef="Dan.8.3">Dan 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.6">Dan 8:6</reference>, “where the kingdom in question stands in the same relation to the flowing river as the four kingdoms in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">Dan 7:2</reference> do to the sea.” For the geographically defined river Ulai has nothing in common with the sea as a symbol of the nations of the world (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.2">Dan 7:2</reference>). The Ulai is rather named as the place where afterwards the ram and the he-goat pushed against one another, and the shock followed, deciding the fate of the Persian kingdom. <div eID="gen15820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15821" type="x-p"/> As, the, the scene of the vision stands in intimate relation to its contents, so also the time at which the revelation was made to Daniel. With the third year of Belshazzar the dynasty of Nebuchadnezzar, the founder of the Babylonian world-kingdom, was extinguished. In this year Belshazzar, the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar, died, and the sovereignty was transferred to a collateral branch, and finally to an intruder, under whom that world-kingdom, once so powerful, in a few years fell to pieces. Shortly before the death of Belshazzar the end of the Babylonian monarchy was thus to be seen, and the point of time, not very remote, which must end the Exile with the fall of Babylon. This point of time was altogether fitted to reveal to the prophet in a vision what would happen after the overthrow of Babylon, and after the termination of the Exile.
entries.8b6ea5934e6ea3a939fe5aec805023d0b96c42c6: <reference osisRef="Dan.8.8">Dan 8:8</reference> <hi type="italic">The transformation of the Javanic kingdom.</hi> - By the kingdom of the ram the he-goat became very great, powerful (הגדּיל as in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.4">Dan 8:4</reference>). But the great horn was broken at the height of his strength, and four similar horns grew up in its stead, toward the four regions of heaven. חזוּת is here used adverbially, <hi type="italic">conspicuously</hi>: there came forth conspicuously four in its place. This statement does not contradict <reference osisRef="Dan.8.22">Dan 8:22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.11.4">Dan 11:4</reference>, according to which the four kingdom shave not the power of the one great horn; for the thought is only this: they represent in themselves a considerable power, without, however, gaining the power of the one undivided kingdom. The breaking of the great horn indicates the breaking up of the monarchy of Alexander by his death. The four horns which grow up in the place of the one great horn are, according to <reference osisRef="Dan.8.22">Dan 8:22</reference>, four kingdoms. These are the dynasties of the Diadochs, of whom there were indeed five: Antigonus, Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus laid claim to the title of king; but for the first time after the overthrow of Antigonus at the battle of Ipsus, 301 b.c., and thus twenty-two years after the death of Alexander (323 b.c.), they became in reality four kings, and so divided the kingdom among themselves, that Lysimachus had Thrace and Bithynia, - Cassander, Macedonia and Greece, - Seleucus, Syria, Babylonia, and the Eastern countries as far as India, - and Ptolemy, Egypt, Palestine, and Arabia Petrea. But from the fact that this first happened after all the descendants of the royal family had been extirpated, we are not to conclude, with Hävernick, that the breaking of the great horn did not denote the death of Alexander, but the extinction of his race or house; a conclusion which derives no valid support from these words of Justin: “All of them abstained from the use of the insignia of this (royal) dignity while the sons of their king survived. So great was their veneration, that although they had royal wealth and resources, they cared not for the name of kings so long as there existed a legitimate heir to Alexander” (<hi type="italic">Hist</hi>. xv. 2. 13). If the breaking of the horn is placed at the point of time when the horn was powerful, here as well as at <reference osisRef="Dan.11.4">Dan 11:4</reference>, the reference of the words to the sudden death of Alexander in the prime of his days, and when in the very height of his victorious career, cannot be disputed; and by the breaking of the horn we can only understand Alexander’s death, and the breaking up of the kingdom founded by him, although it was still held together in a considerable degree for two decenniums by his generals, till the most imperious and the most powerful amongst them usurped the rank of kings, and then, after the conquest of Antigonus, a formal division of the kingdom into the four considerable kingdoms here named raised them to royal dignity. <div eID="gen15824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15825" type="x-p"/> The prophetic representation is not a prediction of historical details, but it gives only the fundamental traces of the development of the world-kingdoms, and that not in the form of a historiographical prophecy, but only so that it sketches the ground-thoughts of the divinely ordained unfolding of these world-kingdoms. This ideal fundamental thought of the prophecy has so wrought itself out in actual history, that from the one great kingdom, after the death of the founder, in the course of time four considerable kingdoms arise. The number four in the prophetic contemplation comes into view only according to its symbolical idea as the number of the world in its extension toward the four regions of heaven, so that thereby only the thought is declared, that a kingdom embracing the world will fall to ruins in a plurality of kingdoms toward all the regions of heaven (Kliefoth). This has been so historically realized, that out of the wars of the Diadochs for the supremacy four kingdoms arose toward the four regions of the earth into longer duration, - that of Cassander (Macedonia) toward the west, that of Seleucus (Babylonia, etc.) toward the east, that of Lysimachus (Thracia and Bithynia) toward the north, and finally that of Ptolemy (Egypt) toward the south.<note placement="foot">When, on the other hand, Hitzig seeks to explain the prophetic representation, here as well as at <reference osisRef="Dan.11.4">Dan 11:4</reference>, that with or immediately after the death of Alexander his kingdom was divided, by reference to 1 Macc. 1:6, according to which Alexander himself, shortly before his death, divided the kingdom among his generals, he thereby not only misapprehends the ideal character of the prophecy, but does not in the least degree clear up the matter itself. For the passage in 1 Macc. 1:6, which not only Arabic and Persian authors repeat, but also Moses v. Chroene, and even later Greek and Latin historiographers, as Ammian Marcell., has been explained by Curtius (x. 10. 5) as a <hi type="italic">fama vana</hi>, and is proved by Wernsdorf (<hi type="italic">de Fide Librr. Macc</hi>. p. 40 f) and Droysen (<hi type="italic">das Test. Alex. 3te Beilage, zu Gesch. des Hellen</hi>. i.) to be without foundation (cf. Grimm, <hi type="italic">K. ex. Hdb. zu 1 Macc</hi>. 1:6). This may have been originally put into circulation by the partisans of the Hellenic kings, in order to legitimatize their sovereignty in the eyes of the people, as Grimm conjectures; yet the confirmation which the book of Daniel appears to give to it contributed to its wide diffusion by Oriental and Byzantine authors, and the author of the first book of the Maccabees had without doubt the book of Daniel before his eyes in the representation he gives.</note><hi type="italic">The interpretation of the vision.</hi>
entries.940bd2d719125ef8960527c9e421560fcf4b9168: <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Dan 8:9</reference> <div eID="gen15825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15826" type="x-p"/> Without following the development of the four horns further, the prophecy passes over to the little horn, which grew up out of one of the four horns, and gained great significance in relation to the history of the people of God. The masculine forms מהם and יצא (<hi type="italic">out of them came</hi>) are to be explained as a <hi type="italic">constructio ad sensum</hi>. אחת (<hi type="italic">one</hi>) after קרן (<hi type="italic">horn</hi>) is as little superfluous as is the מן in מצּעירה. אחת is a numeral, <hi type="italic">one</hi> horn, not several; מן is either comparative, less than little, i.e., <hi type="italic">very little</hi> (Ewald), or, as less than insignificance, wretchedness, i.e., <hi type="italic">in an altogether miserable way</hi> (Häv.). The one explanation is more forced than the other, and the idea of wretchedness is altogether untenable. Yet the מן serves as a circumlocution for the superlative = <hi type="italic">perpaucus</hi> (Gesen., Win., Aub.), while verbal analogies for it are wanting. מן signifies <hi type="italic">from, out of</hi>; but it is not to be united with קרן: <hi type="italic">one horn of smallness</hi> (v. Leng.), in which case מן would be superfluous, but with the verb יצא: <hi type="italic">it came up out of littleness, a parvo</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">a parvis initiis</hi> (Maur., Hofm., Kran., Klief.). Thus it corresponds with סלקת זעירה, Dan 7:8. In the words “it arose out of littleness” there lies the idea that it grew to great power from a small beginning; for it became very great, i.e., powerful, toward the south, toward the east, and toward the הצּבי (<hi type="italic">the splendour, glory</hi>), i.e., toward the glorious land. הצּבי = הצּבי ארץ, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">Dan 11:16</reference>, Dan 11:41. This designation of the land of Israel is framed after <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jer 3:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.15">Eze 20:15</reference>, where this land is called “a heritage of the greatest glory of nations” (a goodly heritage of the host of nations, E. V.), “a glory of all lands,” i.e., the most glorious land which a people can possess. The expression is synonymous with חמדּה ארץ (“pleasant land”), <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jer 3:19</reference>; Zec 7:14; Psa 106:24. Canaan was so designate don account of its great fruitfulness as a land flowing with milk and honey; cf. Eze 20:6. <div eID="gen15826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15827" type="x-p"/> The one of the four horns from which the little horn grew up is the Syrian monarchy, and the horn growing up out of it is the king Antiochus Epiphanes, as Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. x. 11. 7) and all interpreters acknowledge, on the ground of 1 Macc. 1:10. The south, against which he became great, is Egypt (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.11.5">Dan 11:5</reference> and 1 Macc. 1:16ff.). The east is not Asia (Kranichfeld), but Babylon, and particularly Elymaïs and Armenia, 1 Macc. 1:31, 37; 3:31, 37; 6:1-4, according to which he subdued Elymaïs and overcame Artaxias, king of Armenia (App. Syr. c. 45, 46; Polyb. xxxi. 11). Besides the south and the east, Canaan, the holy land, as lying between, is named as the third land, as in Isa 19:23. it is named as third, between Egypt and Assyria; but הצּבי ואל (“and toward the glorious land”) is not, with Kranichfeld, to be regarded as an exegetical addition to המּזרח ואל (“and toward the east”). Palestine lay neither to the east of Daniel, nor geographically to the east of the kingdom denoted by the little horn, because the text gives no support to the identifying of this kingdom with the Javanic, the horn operating from the west.
entries.b78425ff43e5fd6773f60d6410b3a3df5bf971c9: <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10">Dan 8:10</reference> <div eID="gen15827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15828" type="x-p"/> As this horn became great in extent toward the south and toward the east, so also it grew up in height even unto the host of heaven, and some of them it cast down, i.e., some of the stars, to the earth. <hi type="italic">The host of heaven</hi> is here, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.33.22">Jer 33:22</reference>, the whole body of the stars of heaven, the constellations, and <hi type="italic">of the stars</hi> is epexegetical of <hi type="italic">of the host</hi>. Daniel in the vision sees the horn grow so great in height, that it reaches even to the heavens, can reach the heavenly bodies with the hand, and throws some of the stars (מן is partitive) down to the earth and tramples upon them, destroys them with scorn. The words of the angel, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.24">Jer 33:24</reference>, show that by the stars we are to understand the people of the saints, the people of God. The stars cast down to the earth are, according to this, neither the Levites (Grotius), nor the <hi type="italic">viri illustres</hi> in Israel (Glass.), nor the chief rulers of the Jews in church and state (Dathe). If the people of the saints generally are compared to the host of heaven, the stars, then the separate stars cannot be the ecclesiastical or civil chiefs, but the members of this nation in common. But by “the people of the saints” is to be understood (since the little horn denotes Antiochus Epiphanes) the people of God in the Old Covenant, the people of Israel. They are named the people of the saints by virtue of their being called to be an holy nation (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>), because “they had the revelation of God and God Himself dwelling among them, altogether irrespective of the subjective degrees of sanctification in individuals” (Kliefoth). But the comparing of them with the host of the stars does not arise from Jewish national pride, nor does it mean that Daniel thought only of the truly faithful in Israel (Theod., Häv.), or that the pseudo-Daniel thought that with the death of Antiochus the Messiah would appear, and that then Israel, after the extermination of the godless, would become a people of pure holiness. The comparison rather has its roots in this, that God, the King of Israel, is called the God of hosts, and by the צבאות (<hi type="italic">hosts</hi>) are generally to be understood the stars or the angels; but the tribes of Israel also, who were led by God out of Egypt, are called “the hosts of Jehovah” (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.4">Exo 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Exo 12:41</reference>). As in heaven the angels and stars, so on earth the sons of Israel form the host of God; and as the angels on account of the glory of their nature are called קדושׁים (<hi type="italic">holy ones</hi>), so the Israelites by virtue of their being chosen to be the holy nation of God, forming the kingdom of heaven in this world. As God, the King of this people, has His throne in heaven, so there also Israel have their true home, and are in the eyes of God regarded as like unto the stars. This comparison serves, then, to characterize the insolence of Antiochus as a wickedness against Heaven and the heavenly order of things. Cf. 2 Macc. 9:10.<note placement="foot">The deep practical explanation of Calvin deserves attention: - ”Although the church often lies prostrate in the world and is trodden under foot, yet is it always precious before God. Hence the prophet adorns the church with this remarkable praise, not to obtain for it great dignity in the sight of men, but because God has separated it from the world and provided for it a sure inheritance in heaven. Although the sons of God are pilgrims on the earth, and have scarcely any place in it, because they are as castaways, yet they are nevertheless citizens of heaven. Hence we derive this useful lesson, that we should bear it patiently when we are thrown prostrate on the ground, and are despised by tyrants and contemners of God. In the meantime our seat is laid up in heaven, and God numbers us among the stars, although, as Paul says, we are as dung and as the offscourings of all things.” - Calv. <hi type="italic">in loc</hi>.</note>
entries.7e063134c7ca7f658a63dfae2efb9496721f941d: <reference osisRef="Dan.8.11">Dan 8:11</reference> <div eID="gen15828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15829" type="x-p"/> This horn raised its might even to the Prince of the host. הצבא שׂר, <hi type="italic">the Prince of the host of heaven</hi>, is obviously not the high priest Onias (Grotius), but the God of heaven and the King of Israel, the Prince of princes, as He is called in Dan 8:25. עד הגדּיל (<hi type="italic">he magnified himself to</hi>) is repeated in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.25">Dan 8:25</reference> by על יעמוד (<hi type="italic">he shall stand up against</hi>). Wherein this rising up against God consisted, the second half of the verse indicates in the statement that the תּמיד (<hi type="italic">daily</hi> sacrifice) was taken away, and the building of His sanctuary was destroyed. This verse does not record a part of the vision, but is a further development of that which was seen in prophetic words. Hence we may not, with Ebrard, refer its contents to heavenly events, to a putting away of the sacrifice from before the throne of God and a destruction of the heavenly sanctuary. On the contrary, Kliefoth has well remarked that it is “without example in Scripture that men penetrate into heaven to insult God; what men do against God is done on the earth.” התּמיד is everything in the worship of God which is not used merely temporarily, but is permanent, as the daily sacrifice, the setting forth of the shew-bread, and the like. The limitation of it to the daily morning and evening service in the writings of the Rabbis is unknown in the O.T. The word much rather comprehends <hi type="italic">all that is of permanent use in the holy services of divine worship</hi> (Hgst., Häv., Hofm., Kran., Klief.). Thus interpreted, the prophetic announcement corresponds with history; for, according to 1 Macc. 1:45, Antiochus gave orders that they should “forbid burnt-offerings, and sacrifice, and drink-offerings in the temple; and that they should profane the Sabbath and festival days.” <div eID="gen15829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15830" type="x-p"/> The horn also overthrew the place of the sanctuary of Jehovah. השׁליך, <hi type="italic">to cast away, to cast forth</hi>, - used of buildings, <hi type="italic">to lay waste</hi>; cf. Jer 9:18. מכון, properly, <hi type="italic">that which is set up</hi>, erected; here, as frequently, of the dwelling-place of God, <hi type="italic">the temple</hi>: so also שׁבתּך מכון (<hi type="italic">a settled place for thee to dwell in</hi>), <reference osisRef="Exod.15.17">Exo 15:17</reference>; 1Ki 8:13. It is used also of the heavenly dwelling-place of God, 1Ki 8:39, 1Ki 8:43; here, of the temple of Jerusalem. With regard to the historical fulfilment, cf. The expressions, “her (Jerusalem’s) sanctuary was laid waste like a wilderness,” and “pollute the sanctuary,” 1 Macc. 1:39, 46; and “the sanctuary was trodden down,” 1 Macc. 3:45.
entries.58be13b4fdfd3d4e9a4cd5ada7d126059c2cac23: <reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Dan 8:12</reference> <div eID="gen15830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15831" type="x-p"/> The actions of the little horn are definitively comprehended in this verse, as may be seen from this, that in the first hemistich צבא and תּמיד are mentioned together. But this hemistich has been very variously interpreted. We must altogether reject the interpretation of the Vulgate, ”<hi type="italic">Robur autem datum est contra juge sacrificium propter peccata,”</hi> which is reproduced in Luther’s translation, <hi type="italic">“</hi>There was given to him such strength against the daily sacrifice on account of sin;” or Calvin’s, ”<hi type="italic">Et tempus datum est super jugi sacrificio in scelere,”</hi> whereby, after Raschi’s example, צבא is interpreted of the <hi type="italic">statio militaris</hi>, and thence the interpretation <hi type="italic">tempus</hi> or <hi type="italic">intervallum</hi> is derived. For צבא means neither <hi type="italic">robur</hi>, nor <hi type="italic">tempus</hi>, nor <hi type="italic">statio militaris</hi>, but only <hi type="italic">military service</hi>, and perhaps <hi type="italic">military forces</hi>. Add to this that צבא both in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10">Dan 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference> means <hi type="italic">host</hi>. If we maintain this, with the majority of interpreters, only two explanations are admissible, according as we understand צבא of the host of heaven, i.e., of Israel, or of some other host. The latter interpretation is apparently supported partly by the absence of the article in צבא, and partly by the construction of the word as fem. (תּנּתן). Accordingly, Hitzig says that a Hebrew reader could not understand the words otherwise than as meaning, <hi type="italic">“</hi>and a warlike expedition was made or conducted against the daily sacrifice with wickedness” (i.e., the impure service of idols); while others translate, “and a host placed against he daily sacrifice on account of sin” (Syr., Grot., Harenb., J. D. Michaelis); or, “a host is given against the daily sacrifice in wickedness” (Wieseler); or, “given against that which was continual with the service of idols,” i.e., so that, in the place of the “continual,” wickedness, the worship of idols, is appointed (Hofmann); or, “the power of an army is given to it (the horn) against the daily sacrifice through wickedness,” i.e., by the evil higher demons (Ebrard). But the latter interpretation is to be rejected on account of the arbitrary insertion of לו (<hi type="italic">to it</hi>); and against all the others it is to be remarked, that there is no proof either from <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference>, or from <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.23">Eze 32:23</reference> or <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.8">Eze 26:8</reference>, that נתן means to lead out, to bring forward, to give contrary to or against.
entries.2d6fd782cb2e24328337acc41cf31131463e994f: <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13-Dan.8.14">Dan 8:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen15831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15832" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference> תּת (<hi type="italic">to give</hi>) is more closely defined by מרמס (<hi type="italic">something trodden under foot</hi>); but in these passages in Ezekiel above referred to, it [the verb נתן] is connected with an actual object. Construed with the <hi type="italic">accus. pers.</hi> and על, נתן means “to place one over anything.” This conception in its different shades is not so much derived from the words of the text as from a reference to the history; for it is supposed (cf. Grotius, Wies.) that because the matter spoken of is the wickedness of Antiochus, the entrance of the Syrian army into Jerusalem and its proceedings (1 Macc. 1:29ff.) must be set forth. צבא, notwithstanding the want of the article, and notwithstanding the feminine construction, cannot properly be otherwise understood in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Dan 8:12</reference> than in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10">Dan 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference>, not of the host of the Syrians, but only of the people of Israel. The article is wanting also in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference>, where yet, because of its being taken in connection with קדשׁ, it can only refer to Israel. Besides this passage, the fem. construction is found also only in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Isa 40:2</reference>, where it signifies the service of war or vassalage. But this meaning here, where weighty reasons oppose it, this construction does not require us to adopt, for such a construction is not infrequent. It is found not merely with names of nations and races, so far as land and people are nearly related ideas, but also with other words, such as even עם, <hi type="italic">people, fem.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.5.16">Exo 5:16</reference>; 1Ki 18:7; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.5">Jer 8:5</reference>; המון, <hi type="italic">a multitude</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.34">Job 31:34</reference>; זרע, <hi type="italic">seed</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">descendants</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference>; cf. Ewald’s <hi type="italic">Lehr</hi>. §174. But the want of the article in צבא in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Dan 8:12</reference> and in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference> has its reason in this, that that which is said does not concern the whole host, but only one part of it, since, according to <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10">Dan 8:10</reference>, the hostile horn will cast only some הצבא מן (<hi type="italic">of the host</hi>) to the earth. If, therefore, there is no sufficient ground for rejecting the application of the צבא to the people of Israel, it follows that this interpretation is decidedly required not only by the connection, chiefly by <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference>, but also by that which is said of צבא in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Dan 8:12</reference></hi>. “Since in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference> the inquirer resumes the contents of <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10-Dan.8.12">Dan 8:10-12</reference>, and along with the sanctuary names also the 'host' as the object of the 'treading down,' it is not credible that this 'host' should be different from that mentioned in Dan 8:12” (Klief.). Moreover, תּנּתן can have in this passage only the meaning of <hi type="italic">to be given up</hi>. התּמיד על can then only be translated <hi type="italic">because of the permanent sacrifice</hi>, if בּפשׁע (<hi type="italic">by reason of transgression</hi>) is united as object with תּנּתן in the sense: “was delivered up in transgression.” But apart from this, that נתן in the sense of <hi type="italic">to give up</hi> is construed with בּיד, and there are wanting certain parallels for its construction with ב merely, this interpretation, “the host (= Israel) is given up in wickedness on account of the continual sacrifice,” presents an idea not to be tolerated. We agree, therefore, in general with the interpretation of Daniel B. Michaelis, Hävernick, v. Lengerke, Maurer, Kranichfeld, and Kliefoth, and explain the words thus: “and (an) host shall be given up together with the daily sacrifice, because of transgression.” צבא, <hi type="italic">an host</hi>, i.e., a great company of the host, the people of Israel. ב before פּשׁע (<hi type="italic">transgression</hi>) in the meaning of ב <hi type="italic">pretii</hi>, <hi type="italic">on account of </hi>(<hi type="italic">um</hi>), or <hi type="italic">because of</hi>, cf. Gen 18:28. פּשׁע is the apostasy of the Israelites from God, the wickedness proceeding from the פּשׁעים (<hi type="italic">transgressors</hi>), Dan 8:23. The objection that this interpretation is not appropriate, because פּשׁע is repeated in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan 8:13</reference> in union with שׁמם (<hi type="italic">desolation</hi>), and therefore a wickedness devoted to destruction is characterized (Klief.), avails nothing, because it in no way follows from this that the “transgression” must be wickedness seating itself in the place of the “daily sacrifice,” idolatrous worship supplanting the true worship. But “the transgression” cannot be that which sets itself in the place of the “daily sacrifice,” because התּמיד is not the subject of the sentence, but is only co-ordinated to the subject. If ב in בּפשׁע is regarded as the ב <hi type="italic">pretii</hi>, then פשׁע can only be that which would be put in the place of the צבא. The preposition על before התּמיד means <hi type="italic">thereon</hi>, <hi type="italic">after that</hi>, also <hi type="italic">at the same time</hi>, or <hi type="italic">together with</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">Amo 3:15</reference>; Hos 10:14, etc. תּמיד, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.11">Dan 8:11</reference>, is not merely the <hi type="italic">daily sacrifice</hi>, but all that had continuance in the Mosaic worship. Finally, the jussive forms תּנּתן and תּשׁלך d (<hi type="italic">to be trodden</hi>) are to be observed, since, according to the just observation of Kran., they are not simply identical with the future, as Ewald (§343) thinks, but here, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.11.4">Dan 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.10">Dan 11:10</reference>,<reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">Dan 11:16</reference>, modify the conception of time by the presentation of the divine pre-determination or the decree, and thus express <hi type="italic">a should</hi>, <hi type="italic">may</hi>, or a <hi type="italic">faculty</hi>, <hi type="italic">a being able</hi>, in consequence of the divine counsel. To the verbs of the second half of the verse קרן (<hi type="italic">horn</hi>) is easily supplied from the foregoing context as the subject; and the passage closes with the thought: thus must the horn throw the truth to the ground, and he shall succeed in this.<note placement="foot">”<hi type="italic">Successus Antiochi potuit pios omnes turbare, acsi tyrannus ille esset Deo superior. Ergo oportuit etiam hoc praedici, ne quid novum vel inopinatum constingeret fidelibus.”</hi> - Calvin.</note> אמת, the objective truth, the word of God, so far as it is embodied in the worship. As to this matter cf. 1 Macc. 1:43-52, 56, 60.  <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13-Dan.8.14">Dan 8:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen15832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15833" type="x-p"/> In addition to what has been already seen and communicated in the vision, a further vision unfolds itself, by which there is conveyed to the prophet disclosures regarding the duration of the oppression of the people of God by the little horn. Daniel hears a holy one, i.e., an angel (see under <reference osisRef="Dan.4.10">Dan 4:10</reference>), talking. What he said is not recorded. But while he is talking, another angel interrupts him with the question as to the duration of the affliction, and this is done that Daniel may hear the answer. Therefore the first angel immediately turns himself to Daniel, and, addressing him, makes known to him the information that was desired. <div eID="gen15833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15834" type="x-p"/> The אלי (<hi type="italic">to me</hi>), <reference osisRef="Dan.8.14">Dan 8:14</reference>, is not, according to the old versions, to be changed into אליו (<hi type="italic">to him</hi>). What Hitzig says in justification of אליו is of no weight; cf. Kran. The angel that talked is designated by פּלמוני, <hi type="italic">quidam, nescio quis</hi>, as not being more particularly definable. The question condenses the contents of <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10-Dan.8.12">Dan 8:10-12</reference> : <hi type="italic">“</hi>Till how long is the vision, etc.?” החזון is not the action, but the contents of the vision, <hi type="italic">the thing seen</hi>. The contents of the vision are arranged in the form of appositions: that which is continual and the desolating wickedness, for: the vision of that which is continual and of the desolation. The meaning of this apposition is more particularly defined by the further passage following <hi type="italic">asyndetos</hi>: to give up the sanctuary as well as the host to destruction. שׁמם after the definite noun without the article, which is sometimes wanting (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jer 2:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.27">Eze 39:27</reference>; cf. Ew. §293), does not mean being benumbed, confounded, but <hi type="italic">laid waste</hi>, fallen into ruin; thus the wickedness which consists in laying waste. שׁמם cannot be understood transitively, since שׁמם and משׁמם are placed over against each other in Dan 9:27. <div eID="gen15834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15835" type="x-p"/> In the answer, עד is to be interpreted as in the question: till 2300 evening-mornings have been, or have passed, thus: 2300 evening-mornings long, so (=then) the sanctuary is brought into its right state. צדק primarily means to be just, whence the meaning is derived to justify, which is not here suitable, for it must be followed by, from the defilement of the desolation. The restoration of the temple to its right condition is, it is true, at the same time a justification of it from its desolation, and it includes in it the restoration of the permanent worship. <div eID="gen15835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15836" type="x-p"/> The interpretation of the period of time, 2300 evening-mornings, named by the angel is beset with difficulty.
